newsitem.title: UK: Britiish Labour Party rejects pact with unions.
newsitem.headline: Britiish Labour Party rejects pact with unions.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party on Sunday rejected a formal partnership with the trade unions if the party wins the next general election.

Labour's employment spokesman Stephen Byers said the party wanted consensus in the workplace but had no proposals to establish a formal means of consulting with the unions, as called for by one senior union leader.
He told BBC radio: ""We don't believe that setting up a formal machinery of government is the best way forward."
John Edmonds of the GMB union earlier called for a partnership between unions and a Labour government with the setting up of a national forum to discuss matters of mutual concern.

Byers was speaking after the head of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), the unions' umbrella body, said they must develop a more constructive outlook if they want to influence the new-look Labour Party in government.

Labour's close ties to the unions -- a major reason for the party's loss of power in 1979 -- have been loosened under leader Tony Blair since his election in 1994, and TUC general secretary John Monks said the unions could not expect favours from Labour. "Britain desperately needs a new government, but a Labour election will only be the beginning of a new set of challenges for the trade union movement. There will be no cavalry coming over the hill to rescue us," Monks said in a New Year message. Judging by opinion polls, Labour will win the next election, due by May 1997, and take power from a Conservative government that has passed a series of anti-union laws since 1979.
Labour has pledged to introduce a minimum wage and give unions greater recognition rights in the workplace, but it has refused to repeal the Conservatives' union laws.
Membership of the unions grouped in the TUC has halved to below seven million since the mid-1970s.
Monks said "habits of opposition" would have to be broken if the unions were to regain influence.

"But I am determined that we must move from being seen as part of the problem -- however unfairly -- to being part of the solution, working both to improve the lot of those at work and to make the country more prosperous and competitive," he said.

Monks, who has helped restore the unions' credibility since becoming TUC leader in 1993, repeated his call for partnership with industry, listing the creation of "positive working relationships with employers" as a union priority.
